system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Aboriginal Peoples and oral and written expression (core)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area examines how Aboriginal Peoples' human rights and fundamental entitlement to self-determination have been denied since invasion, and the relationship between land rights and Aboriginal Communities' autonomy.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Key concepts of human rights, self-determination and autonomy

Human rights are classified into 3 categories:

  • civil and political rights – held by individuals
  • economic, social and cultural rights – held by individuals
  • collective human rights – held by whole communities and include the right to self-determination, the right to economic and social development, the right to communicate, and the right to a healthy environment and natural resources.

Human rights are about social justice, ensuring the fair and equitable distribution of and access to economic, political, social and cultural rights and opportunities.

Self-determination and autonomy involve allowing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to have a say in all matters that affect them and to have an ongoing choice about what is best for them individually and collectively.

Collective human rights are important for Indigenous Peoples worldwide because many Indigenous Peoples often have a collective worldview, whereby their identity and wellbeing are defined in relation to the whole group.

Denial of human rights

Historically, Indigenous Peoples worldwide have been subjected to human rights violations by colonising powers. In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples were and are impacted by the legacies of invasion, colonisation and the subsequent denial of human rights. These impacts include:

  • inability to make decisions individually and collectively
  • prohibiting the recognition, practice and maintenance of Languages and Cultures
  • intergenerational trauma, including trauma experienced by survivors of the Stolen Generations, their families and Communities
  • disadvantages concerning education, health, employment, economic independence and experiences with law and justice systems.

To address past injustices and ongoing impacts, many Aboriginal Community-controlled organisations, advisory groups and advocacy groups have emerged. These are addressed further in the Aboriginal enterprises and organisations focus area.

Individuals and Communities are reclaiming and revitalising Cultural Knowledges and Practices such as:

  • Language, song, dance and ceremony
  • land and waterway management Practices.

Lands and waterways, economic independence and self-determination

  • As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have had an intrinsic connection to lands and waterways since the beginning of the Dreaming.
  • Waterways may be described as Saltwater and Freshwater Country, but may include lakes, billabongs, estuaries, and surrounding vegetation and landforms.
  • The land and its waterways contain the necessary resources from which Aboriginal Peoples have always sustainably built economic systems, including trade within and outside the continent.
  • Colonisation and dispossession changed the way many Aboriginal Peoples accessed the land, its waterways and resources. This impacted individual and Community opportunities for economic independence and self-determination.

Land rights

Land rights encapsulates the evolving struggle of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Indigenous Peoples worldwide for the absolute legal and moral acknowledgement of prior ownership of their land. This struggle also encompasses all accompanying rights and obligations that flow from this, including economic independence and self-determination.

Native Title

  • ‘Native Title’ is the name given by the High Court to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander property rights recognised by the court in the Mabo judgement. See Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1.
  • The High Court’s Wik judgement (Wik Peoples v The State of Queensland; The Thayorre People v The State of Queensland [1996] HCA 40) decided an issue left unresolved by the Mabo judgement when it determined that native title could coexist with other rights on land held under a pastoral lease.
  • Increasingly, the definition is governed by the terms of the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), amended in 1998.
  • Native Title as recognised by Australian law does not cover the full scope of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ relationship to Country/Place under their laws and has been characterised as ‘recognition space’ between Customary law and Australian law.
  • ‘Native Title’ (capitalised) refers to the legislation, whereas ‘native title’ (lower case) refers to the concept.

Key terms

  • advocacy
  • autonomy
  • Cultural expression(s)
  • freehold title
  • genocide
  • human rights
  • Indigenous Land Use Agreement (ILUA)
  • Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs)
  • land rights
  • Mabo
  • missions
  • Native Title/native title
  • reserves
  • self-determination
  • Stolen Generations
  • terra nullius
  • United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)

Suggested case studies

A case study on the activities of organisations, movements and individuals who have worked towards Aboriginal Peoples' autonomy and the broader Community response can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • Aboriginal Tent Embassy
  • 1967 Referendum.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of issues that have arisen post-invasion and which impact Aboriginal Peoples' demands for self-determination.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for the development of numeracy skills that are relevant to this focus area. For example, analysing data related to population changes in Aboriginal Communities, using maps to record Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land usage and ownership, or exploring timelines that represent the chronology of events and their impacts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes in the focus area Aboriginal Peoples’ interaction with legal and political systems determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about Aboriginal-led initiatives addressing legal and political issues locally, regionally or nationally, the outcome requires them to describe the role of families and Communities for Aboriginal Peoples. Students identify the features of Circle Sentencing and describe how families and Communities support individuals throughout the process.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples’ interaction with legal and political systems. For example, students learn about Aboriginal Community police liaison officers and identify how they are working together, demonstrating respect and building relationships in the local Community.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • the role of the Police Citizens Youth Club (PCYC) in local Aboriginal Communities
  • how laws can keep us safe.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • using concept maps to identify connections between Cultural Practices and Australian Government systems, for example creating graphic organisers to make comparisons between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal legal and political systems
  • using scaffolding such as visual and verbal prompts and sentence starters to support the exploration of participation and representation of Aboriginal Peoples in various forms of government
  • chunking content by breaking down information, focusing on one legal or political practice or process at a time, and providing multiple opportunities for engagement
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Key legal and political structures for maintaining social cohesion and harmony in Aboriginal Cultures by Aboriginal Peoples
The teacher explains how Yarning circles use restorative justice and governance practices to reach consensus and maintain social cohesion. Students investigate how Aboriginal Peoples have been supported by the inclusion of Yarning circles into contemporary legal practices to resolve conflict and reach consensus with the help of family and Elders from their Community.

Life Skills

  • Aboriginal-led initiatives addressing legal and political issues locally, regionally or nationally
The teacher describes what a Yarning circle is and how it is used as a restorative justice practice in Community and school contexts. Students are supported with visuals and manipulatives to understand that everyone is equal in a Yarning circle, meaning that decisions are made collaboratively. Students use sentence starters and prompts to participate in the Yarning circle, with the support of family and Elders from their Community.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area examines the relationships between Aboriginal Peoples and the Australian legal and political systems. Students are introduced to Aboriginal Peoples’ legal and political structures before invasion and the impact of invasion on these structures. Students learn about Aboriginal Peoples’ initiatives and advocacy to access their rights and achieve equity in legal and political systems.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Aboriginal Peoples’ legal and political systems

As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have always observed, adapted and maintained Practices associated with contemporary concepts of law and politics. These include:

  • Customary Lore – sometimes referred to as Traditional Law. Customary Lore details rules, responsibilities and obligations that are deeply connected to the Dreaming, Kinship and Country. These include obligations about totemic connections and interactions with Country and the environment, ceremony, marriage rules, specific gender roles and responsibilities, and expected behaviours and societal interactions.
  • Governance of Elders – as senior Knowledge Holders, Elders are responsible for the oral transmission and governance of Customary Lore and decision-making.
  • Elders are responsible for ensuring that Customary Lore is taught and upheld.
  • Punishments for breaking the rules are discussed by all concerned, with Elders presiding to collectively ensure restorative justice to all involved.

Impact of invasion and colonisation

Terra nullius was one of the very first legal concepts imposed on Aboriginal Peoples to justify the colonisation of Australia. Although it has been overturned, its impact on Aboriginal society has been significant. Dispossession and dislocation from Country and subsequent policies of protection and assimilation disrupted Kinship structures, including the removal of children and the restriction of personal freedoms or autonomy for Aboriginal Peoples. The imposition of new laws saw Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples denied access to all aspects of Country, including Customary Lore and governance practices. Under imposed laws, Elders lost their authority, and punishments did not necessarily bring justice to those involved.

Interactions with legal and political systems

Australia is a representative democracy, constitutional monarchy and a federation. Despite being the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples are a minority group within this system. Aboriginal Peoples and Communities face significant challenges during interactions with legal and political systems, such as:

  • accessibility and affordability
  • Cultural safety
  • negative historical experiences
  • over-representation of Aboriginal Peoples in incarceration rates nationally.

Responses and initiatives

Aboriginal Peoples have always been innovative and solutions-focused in responding to current legal and political trends. Community-led, statewide and national initiatives in response to issues ranging from human rights, land rights, structural reform and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) have delivered positive outcomes for Aboriginal Peoples. The case study for this option provides an opportunity for students to learn about Aboriginal Community-led legal and political initiatives that have demonstrated positive outcomes for their respective Communities.

Key terms

  • Aboriginal Community Liaison Officers (ACLOs)
  • Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS)
  • Circle Sentencing
  • Customary Lore
  • dislocation
  • Elders
  • governance
  • incarceration
  • institutional racism
  • over-representation
  • protectionism
  • restorative justice practices

Suggested case studies

A case study on Aboriginal Community-led legal and political initiatives that have demonstrated positive outcomes for their respective Communities can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs)
  • NSW Aboriginal Land Council.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of issues that have arisen post-invasion which have led to current legal and political trends for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for the development of numeracy skills that are relevant to this focus area. For example using basic network diagrams to represent Kinship connections, using maps to represent the disruption and dislocation of Kinship groups, or using data analysis to assess the positive impacts of Aboriginal Peoples’ initiatives.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes in the focus area Aboriginal Peoples’ interaction with legal and political systems determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about Aboriginal-led initiatives addressing legal and political issues locally, regionally or nationally, the outcome requires them to describe the role of families and Communities for Aboriginal Peoples. Students identify the features of Circle Sentencing and describe how families and Communities support individuals throughout the process.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples’ interaction with legal and political systems. For example, students learn about Aboriginal Community police liaison officers and identify how they are working together, demonstrating respect and building relationships in the local Community.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • the role of the Police Citizens Youth Club (PCYC) in local Aboriginal Communities
  • how laws can keep us safe.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • using concept maps to identify connections between Cultural Practices and Australian Government systems, for example creating graphic organisers to make comparisons between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal legal and political systems
  • using scaffolding such as visual and verbal prompts and sentence starters to support the exploration of participation and representation of Aboriginal Peoples in various forms of government
  • chunking content by breaking down information, focusing on one legal or political practice or process at a time, and providing multiple opportunities for engagement
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Key legal and political structures for maintaining social cohesion and harmony in Aboriginal Cultures by Aboriginal Peoples
The teacher explains how Yarning circles use restorative justice and governance practices to reach consensus and maintain social cohesion. Students investigate how Aboriginal Peoples have been supported by the inclusion of Yarning circles into contemporary legal practices to resolve conflict and reach consensus with the help of family and Elders from their Community.

Life Skills

  • Aboriginal-led initiatives addressing legal and political issues locally, regionally or nationally
The teacher describes what a Yarning circle is and how it is used as a restorative justice practice in Community and school contexts. Students are supported with visuals and manipulatives to understand that everyone is equal in a Yarning circle, meaning that decisions are made collaboratively. Students use sentence starters and prompts to participate in the Yarning circle, with the support of family and Elders from their Community.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes of the focus area Aboriginal Peoples and sport determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about how sport can contribute to positive relationships between Aboriginal Peoples and non-Aboriginal people, the outcome requires them to recognise the relationships between Aboriginal Peoples and non-Aboriginal people. Students identify a range of team sports and explore ways in which being part of a team builds positive connections with others.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples and sport. For example, teachers explicitly teach students to identify and respect the different purposes of Traditional games that prioritise collaborative skills and relationship building.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • Traditional Games (Yulunga/Marn Grook) and contemporary connections – rules, origins and purpose
  • the NSW Aboriginal Rugby League Knockout (Koori Knockout) – origin, history and importance to NSW Aboriginal Communities
  • how to participate in a sporting activity.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • using sequencing activities that include visual and verbal prompts to support engagement with the instructions or rules of a Customary game as spectators, scorers or participants
  • guided practice of collaboration skills such as turn-taking and sharing equipment when engaging in group activities, including sports, engaging with a range of scenarios to build understanding and to apply collaborative skills
  • using scaffolding and graphic organisers to explore a significant Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander sports identity, team or competition, including checklists to guide the research process
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • The contribution of Aboriginal sportspeople as role models locally, nationally and internationally
The teacher introduces well-known Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander individuals and teams and supports students in determining their importance as role models for individuals and communities. Students create a multimodal presentation about an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander sportsperson or sporting team and analyse the impact they have made as role models at local, national and/or international levels.

Life Skills

  • Contributions of Aboriginal sportspeople as role models
The teacher introduces a range of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander sportspeople, teams and competitions. Students create a multimodal presentation about an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander sportsperson, sporting team or competition, identifying their positive impact on individuals and communities.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes in the focus area Aboriginal Peoples and technologies determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about the range of technologies developed and used by Aboriginal Peoples, the outcome requires them to identify the contributions of Aboriginal Peoples in a range of contexts. Students recognise and name material, medical and scientific technology developed and used by Aboriginal Peoples.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples and technologies. For example, teachers demonstrate appropriate respect for Aboriginal Peoples as Custodians of Country and Knowledge Holders by identifying and applying protocols related to the technologies, including associated social and Cultural Practices.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander inventors, for example, David Unaipon
  • how technology has endured and been adapted by modern innovations
  • care for Country – the use of fire
  • the use of tools to solve everyday problems.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • connecting to other learning by making explicit links to other subjects such as Mathematics and Science when exploring how tools such as woomeras are designed and used, or combining units addressing concepts such as forces, speed or sustainability
  • hands-on activities using manipulative resources to support understanding of, and engagement with, tools and technologies
  • using visual supports such as diagrams, mind maps and graphic organisers to support the understanding of the purpose and use of various tools and technologies
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Ways in which Aboriginal Peoples' technologies are an integral part of Aboriginal social and Cultural Practices
The teacher introduces various tools and techniques and demonstrates how social and Cultural Practices guide the use and application of these technologies. Students participate in an on-Country experience to engage with Elders to further understand Aboriginal Peoples’ technologies. They conduct an analysis of the use of the tools and techniques and the relationship to social and Cultural Practices.

Life Skills

  • Use of Aboriginal Peoples' technologies in Aboriginal social and Cultural Practices
The teacher introduces various tools and techniques and demonstrates how social and Cultural Practices guide the use and application of these technologies. Students participate in an on-Country experience to engage with Elders to further understand Aboriginal Peoples’ technologies. They select one tool and identify its purpose, who used it and the way it was used.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes in the focus area Aboriginal Peoples and film and television determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about positive representations of Aboriginal Peoples and/or Cultures in film and television, the outcome requires them to identify how representations of Aboriginal Peoples in Australian society influence the perceptions of non-Aboriginal people. Students engage with excerpts from film or television that provide positive representations and identify new learning about Aboriginal Peoples and Cultures.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples and film and television. For example, teachers guide students to engage with original films (including short films) crafted from Aboriginal perspectives and that demonstrate respect and appreciation for Language, Cultures and lived experiences.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander actors
  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander filmmakers, television directors, television content managers, production companies
  • how film and television can tell stories.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • multiple opportunities to engage with positive representations of Aboriginal Peoples and Cultures in film and television, including examples of media that are owned or controlled by Aboriginal Peoples and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • using who, what, where, when, why and how questions about a film or television excerpt, supported with a visual checklist or prompts
  • explicit teaching about roles and stereotypes, using a range of familiar examples and descriptions, and encouraging students to identify ways to challenge stereotypes
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Positive outcomes of representations of Aboriginal Peoples in film and television, including self-determination and autonomy
The teacher guides students to identify an Aboriginal actor on mainstream television who has been nominated for an award for outstanding achievements in their industry. Students are supported in learning about the actor’s journey and identifying their achievements, successes and challenges. They create a written text explaining how the nominations and recognition in the television industry may have affected the perceptions of non-Aboriginal people.

Life Skills

  • The benefits of Aboriginal Peoples' roles in film and television
Students identify an Aboriginal actor on mainstream television who has been nominated for an award for outstanding achievements in their industry. The teacher provides resources for students to learn about the actor’s journey and identify achievements, successes and challenges. Students create an oral, visual, written or multimodal text identifying the positive impact of this individual on the perceptions of non-Aboriginal people.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Before studying this focus area, students may need an understanding of the factors that shape Aboriginal identities and Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy.

Focus of study

The outcomes in the focus area Aboriginal Peoples and the media determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when learning about examples of media that provide positive representations of Aboriginal Peoples and/or Cultures, the outcome requires students to identify how representations of Aboriginal Peoples in Australian society influence the perceptions of non-Aboriginal people. Students consider Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander media personalities and identify how they are positive role models for all members of society.

Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions

The content group Respect, sharing and Custodianship of Cultural expressions is unique to Life Skills. Teachers can select content that is appropriate to the needs, strengths and prior learning of individual students in the context of Aboriginal Peoples and the media. For example, teachers demonstrate respect by following appropriate protocols while investigating the changes in the language and images used to represent Aboriginal Peoples and Culture over time in advertising.

Case studies

Consulting and collaborating with local Aboriginal Communities will ensure local Practices are embedded in schools and classrooms in a Culturally inclusive, respectful and informed way. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural protocols set out appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect when engaging with Aboriginal Peoples and local Aboriginal Communities (see Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols).

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to engage in a case study related to a person, group or event.

Considerations may include:

  • an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander media identity
  • a media organisation or enterprise that is owned or controlled by Aboriginal Peoples and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • how media is used to share information, stories, histories and perspectives.

Engagement in case studies may be supported by connecting to areas of student interest or prior learning. Teachers should also provide opportunities for students to communicate learning using their preferred communication form(s) and encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports, where appropriate, and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.

Teaching and learning

Teaching strategies to support student learning could include:

  • explicit teaching of key words and concepts such as bias, racism, stereotypes and representation using a range of visual, written and digital resources
  • developing a supportive classroom environment by establishing clear guidelines and expectations when discussing stereotyping and media contexts, using visual and verbal prompts where appropriate
  • providing opportunities for students to engage with media and explore positive representations of Aboriginal Peoples and Culture, including visual, written and digital forms, and media owned or controlled by Aboriginal Peoples and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • explicit teaching of research skills to support the case study, including the use of effective search terms, identifying reliable sources and using note-taking scaffolds.

Connecting with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies

Teachers may need to program Life Skills content alongside Stage 5 content to meet the needs of various students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Aboriginal Studies outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Aboriginal Studies in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Contemporary use of media by Aboriginal Peoples in presenting a balanced view of Aboriginal Peoples, histories and Cultures
The teacher presents a range of NAIDOC posters and support students to identify aspects of Aboriginal Peoples’ histories and Cultures. They explore social and political issues expressed through the images and words. Students create a written text to explain why and how the NAIDOC posters maintain and celebrate Aboriginal Peoples’ identity and Cultures.

Life Skills

  • Representations of Aboriginal Peoples and/or Aboriginal Cultures in the media
Students select one NAIDOC poster and are supported to recognise how Aboriginal Peoples are represented by identifying images and language that reflect Aboriginal Peoples’ identity or Cultures.

Content focus

This focus area examines the establishment and diversity of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations. Students learn about the concepts of autonomy and governance, the roles of a range of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations and the impacts these enterprises and organisations have on social justice and self-determination for Aboriginal Peoples and Communities.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Aboriginal Peoples' autonomy and governance

As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have always had sophisticated societal structures. Each member of society had a role determined by knowledge and gender. Families lived in smaller groups and were linked to larger Language Groups through sophisticated Kinship structures and intrinsic connections to Country. Relationships within and between Language Groups and with outsiders were based on concepts of respect, responsibility and reciprocity, and governed by Traditional Lore. Aboriginal society was governed by the authority of Elders, senior Custodians of Knowledge and Lore. There is no word for 'leader' in many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages. Leadership and governance in Aboriginal Communities was complex for the following reasons.

  • No single person was in charge. Instead, Communities were governed by a group of Elders with varied levels of knowledge, experience and responsibility.
  • Gender and age were important factors. However, while age was important, the level of knowledge and respect was also important. This is particularly important for matters of Men's and Women's Business.
  • All decisions were based on what was best for the collective rather than for individuals.

Invasion and colonisation interrupted Aboriginal Peoples’ rights to autonomy and the ability to self-govern; there was little understanding of Aboriginal society and Knowledge systems. The British claimed 'ownership' of the country based on the doctrine of terra nullius and imposed new systems of governance, which impacted Aboriginal Peoples and society in the following ways.

  • Kinship systems were disrupted, leading to intergenerational trauma as families and Communities were separated from each other and Country.
  • Connections to Country were disrupted due to dispossession, dislocation, protectionism and movement of Peoples onto missions and managed reserves (often off-Country for those being moved).
  • Language, Lore, ceremony and Customary Practices were forbidden.
  • Imposed systems of governance and law did not recognise the complexity of Aboriginal societies. Elders were no longer responsible, and responsibility now lay with non-Aboriginal state lawmakers and governors.
  • Aboriginal Peoples were disempowered and forced to rely on welfare.

Image long description: A series of 4 concentric circles, with each circle nested within the circle larger than it. In order of largest to smallest, the circles are labelled Community; Elders; Culture, Kinship, Laws, Responsibilities & Obligations; and Country & Lore.

Diversity of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations

Aboriginal enterprises and organisations are uniquely positioned to support Aboriginal Peoples and Communities. These enterprises and organisations often act as conduits between non-Aboriginal organisations, government policy and legislation, and Aboriginal Peoples and Communities. These enterprises and organisations:

  • are Aboriginal Community-controlled and staffed
  • promote, create and support Aboriginal self-determination, autonomy and empowerment
  • place the needs of Aboriginal Peoples, their Families and Communities at the forefront
  • support Aboriginal ways of Knowing, Being, Doing and valuing, including the reclamation and revitalisation of Cultural Practices and Aboriginal Languages
  • provide and promote Cultural safety
  • support accountability
  • provide employment opportunities for Aboriginal Peoples
  • provide social and emotional wellbeing support services, including support for those impacted by the Stolen Generations and intergenerational trauma
  • provide Culturally appropriate support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to navigate institutions and services, such as those addressing legal, financial, medical, housing and educational matters.

Key terms

  • Aboriginal Community organisations
  • Aboriginal-controlled
  • Aboriginal enterprises
  • autonomy
  • governance
  • Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP)
  • not-for-profit
  • self-determination
  • Stolen Generations

Suggested case studies

A case study on the activities of an Aboriginal enterprise or organisation can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • NSW Aboriginal Education Consultative Group Inc (AECG)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area examines the establishment and diversity of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations. Students learn about the concepts of autonomy and governance, the roles of a range of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations and the impacts these enterprises and organisations have on social justice and self-determination for Aboriginal Peoples and Communities.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Aboriginal Peoples' autonomy and governance

As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have always had sophisticated societal structures. Each member of society had a role determined by knowledge and gender. Families lived in smaller groups and were linked to larger Language Groups through sophisticated Kinship structures and intrinsic connections to Country. Relationships within and between Language Groups and with outsiders were based on concepts of respect, responsibility and reciprocity, and governed by Traditional Lore. Aboriginal society was governed by the authority of Elders, senior Custodians of Knowledge and Lore. There is no word for 'leader' in many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages. Leadership and governance in Aboriginal Communities was complex for the following reasons.

  • No single person was in charge. Instead, Communities were governed by a group of Elders with varied levels of knowledge, experience and responsibility.
  • Gender and age were important factors. However, while age was important, the level of knowledge and respect was also important. This is particularly important for matters of Men's and Women's Business.
  • All decisions were based on what was best for the collective rather than for individuals.

Invasion and colonisation interrupted Aboriginal Peoples’ rights to autonomy and the ability to self-govern; there was little understanding of Aboriginal society and Knowledge systems. The British claimed 'ownership' of the country based on the doctrine of terra nullius and imposed new systems of governance, which impacted Aboriginal Peoples and society in the following ways.

  • Kinship systems were disrupted, leading to intergenerational trauma as families and Communities were separated from each other and Country.
  • Connections to Country were disrupted due to dispossession, dislocation, protectionism and movement of Peoples onto missions and managed reserves (often off-Country for those being moved).
  • Language, Lore, ceremony and Customary Practices were forbidden.
  • Imposed systems of governance and law did not recognise the complexity of Aboriginal societies. Elders were no longer responsible, and responsibility now lay with non-Aboriginal state lawmakers and governors.
  • Aboriginal Peoples were disempowered and forced to rely on welfare.

Image long description: A series of 4 concentric circles, with each circle nested within the circle larger than it. In order of largest to smallest, the circles are labelled Community; Elders; Culture, Kinship, Laws, Responsibilities & Obligations; and Country & Lore.

Diversity of Aboriginal enterprises and organisations

Aboriginal enterprises and organisations are uniquely positioned to support Aboriginal Peoples and Communities. These enterprises and organisations often act as conduits between non-Aboriginal organisations, government policy and legislation, and Aboriginal Peoples and Communities. These enterprises and organisations:

  • are Aboriginal Community-controlled and staffed
  • promote, create and support Aboriginal self-determination, autonomy and empowerment
  • place the needs of Aboriginal Peoples, their Families and Communities at the forefront
  • support Aboriginal ways of Knowing, Being, Doing and valuing, including the reclamation and revitalisation of Cultural Practices and Aboriginal Languages
  • provide and promote Cultural safety
  • support accountability
  • provide employment opportunities for Aboriginal Peoples
  • provide social and emotional wellbeing support services, including support for those impacted by the Stolen Generations and intergenerational trauma
  • provide Culturally appropriate support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to navigate institutions and services, such as those addressing legal, financial, medical, housing and educational matters.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area addresses the diversity of Aboriginal Cultures and identities and the factors contributing to their maintenance and expression.

Aboriginal Cultures and identities content develops knowledge and understanding about appropriate consultation protocols and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP), so students can work ethically with their local Aboriginal Communities.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Spiritual identity

  • The Dreamtime can potentially be used to describe a specific period that has concluded where the Dreamings are continuous and still very much a part of contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander spiritual beliefs.
  • The term ‘spirituality’ or ‘spiritual beliefs’ is more appropriate when referring to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander spiritual Practices, which are strongly linked to Country and centred on a strong feeling of connectedness and belonging to the land and environment.
  • Spirituality is deeply connected to the identity of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. The term ‘religion’ is not appropriate for describing the spirituality of Aboriginal Peoples. It is important to understand that many Aboriginal People embrace mainstream religion and blend this with their spirituality.
  • When referring to Torres Strait Islander Cultures and beliefs, the correct term is the ‘Legends', whereas 'Dreaming', 'Dreaming stories' and/or 'Creation stories' are more appropriate terms to use when referring to Aboriginal Peoples' beliefs. As a mark of respect, it is important to capitalise these terms. It is advisable to avoid words such as 'myth' or 'story' as standalone terms, as they may create the impression that elements of the Dreaming are fictional and only occurred in the past. Such terminology may also cause people to view Dreaming stories and Legends as fairytales rather than important elements of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander spirituality that are ongoing and present in everyday life.

Family structures

  • Family and Kinship structures are complex and diverse in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities. These structures involve more than just extended family and biological relationships. These structures establish how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples relate to each other and their environment, maintaining Culture and forming interconnected and balanced Communities.
  • In a Kinship system, everyone has a place and a role. Systems can follow either a matrilineal line or a patrilineal line. For example, in New South Wales, matrilineal Kinship lines are often, but not always, observed. Therefore, all rights, responsibilities and obligations to Country and People are based on the ancestral connections of an individual's mother's line. However, it is important to remember that this may vary between Language Groups – patrilineal lines may also be important for families.
  • All Aboriginal People who hold a position in a Kinship system have a responsibility and Cultural obligation to adhere to and uphold Kinship principles through their actions with People and Country.
  • It is important to remind students that many Aboriginal Peoples are reclaiming this knowledge due to past policies and practices. Despite this, a Kinship system is practised in many Aboriginal Language Groups, and all members understand their rights, responsibilities and obligations from a young age. Therefore, engaging with local Aboriginal Community Knowledge Holders is essential to ensure the correct terminology and protocols are followed when discussing Kinship matters.
  • When exploring concepts of family structures and Kinship in Aboriginal Communities, it is important to remember that there may be a diverse range of student contexts in your classroom. Therefore, teachers should be sensitive to this when asking students to share personal stories or other information.

Key terms

  • Aboriginal Peoples
  • Community/Communities
  • Country/Place
  • Cultural expression(s)
  • Customary adoption (Ailan Kustom child-rearing Practices)
  • dispossession
  • diversity
  • Dreaming stories
  • Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP)
  • Kinship
  • Legends of the Torres Strait
  • matrilineal
  • patrilineal
  • spiritual(ity)
  • stereotypes
  • Stolen Generations
  • Torres Strait Islander Peoples

Suggested case studies

A case study on Aboriginal Community identities can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • AIATSIS (Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies)
  • Language and Culture revitalisation initiatives.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of issues that have arisen post-invasion and their effect on Aboriginal identities.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for the development of numeracy skills that are relevant to this focus area. For example, using basic network diagrams to explore concepts of family structures and Kinship in Aboriginal Communities, using maps to record Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages, or exploring how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ intricate knowledge of the environment is represented in seasonal calendars.

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Aboriginal identities (core)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This option focuses on exploring oral and written forms of communication used by Aboriginal Peoples before and after invasion as ways of Cultural expression. Students examine various forms of oral and written expressions to develop an understanding of the diversity of styles and viewpoints, and the importance of these expressions to the development of individual and national identities, histories and Cultures. Throughout the study of this content, students learn to apply ethical research and skills, including protocols for consultation and working effectively and respectfully with their local Aboriginal Community(ies).

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Oral expression

  • Aboriginal Peoples have always practised Oral traditions.
  • Oral Storytelling traditions through sharing Cultural Practices, including connections to Country, Dreaming and Lore, and song and ceremony, are an essential way to maintain historical records and to sustain Culture and identity.
  • These traditions are essential in handing down Knowledges, values, histories and lived experiences from older generations to younger ones, ensuring continuity.
  • Oral traditions are valuable for developing relationships between Aboriginal Peoples and non-Aboriginal people, promoting respect and deeper shared understandings.
  • Oral traditions validate past, present and future links between oral and written histories.

Impact of invasion and colonisation

  • Language and Culture are inseparable. Language is the vehicle for expressing Cultural values and beliefs, and understanding social expectations.
  • Invasion and colonisation of Australia significantly impacted oral expressions of Aboriginal Peoples, including imposed Languages and the banning of Cultural Practices, such as Aboriginal Languages, songs and ceremonies.
  • Despite these impacts, Aboriginal Languages, including handtalk, have survived and others are being reclaimed and revitalised.
  • Strong Cultural connections have supported the survival of Aboriginal Languages, with many Communities now leading the work in preserving, reclaiming and revitalising Aboriginal Languages in New South Wales.
  • Aboriginal English is now recognised as an important aspect of Aboriginal Cultures, representing the unique identity, history and worldview of Aboriginal Communities.
  • Aboriginal Languages, including Aboriginal English, empower Aboriginal Communities, and foster pride, self-esteem and a sense of belonging, which is vital for maintaining Cultural heritage and passing down Knowledge and wisdom through Oral traditions intergenerationally.

Adaptation of oral expression to written forms

Aboriginal Peoples have adapted their Oral traditions to include contemporary technologies, embracing a variety of written or text mediums, including:

  • visual and performing arts mediums
  • digital media, including radio, film and television
  • electronic language mediums such as dictionaries and digital apps
  • literary mediums such as prose, poetry and scripted works.

These adaptations have empowered Aboriginal Peoples and enabled the sharing of Aboriginal Cultures, Knowledges, Languages and lived experiences with wider audiences. Essential considerations include:

  • Aboriginal Cultures and heritages are significant to the nation.
  • Cultural teachings are embedded in Languages, stories, songs and ceremonies of Aboriginal Peoples, connecting individuals to their identity and Country.
  • Preserving Oral traditions is integral to the continuity and resilience of Aboriginal Cultures and the challenges imposed by colonisation and modernity.
  • Aboriginal Peoples’ Oral traditions have never been static, and have always allowed for subtle changes over time. Adapting Aboriginal oral expressions to written forms is another way of intergenerationally preserving and sharing Cultural heritage, history and Knowledges. This adaptation continues to maintain the integrity of stories, traditions and Languages, ensuring they are within reach of a broader audience and preventing their loss or distortion over time.
  • These adaptations also aid in nurturing a deeper understanding and appreciation of Aboriginal Cultures and their invaluable contributions to Australia's shared history and heritage as a nation.

Key terms

  • Aboriginal Language dictionaries
  • Aboriginal Languages
  • adaptation(s)
  • Cultural Knowledges
  • disconnection
  • handtalk
  • heritages
  • Oral histories
  • Place-based
  • Sacred sites
  • Songlines
  • totemic systems
  • written forms

Suggested case studies

A case study on the local Aboriginal Community and the oral and written expressions can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • Aboriginal-owned and operated publishers
  • oral narratives in the local Aboriginal Community(ies)
  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander award-winning writers.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of the importance of oral and written expression in maintaining Aboriginal Cultures.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.

title.value: Teaching advice for Aboriginal Peoples and oral and written expression (core)

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Aboriginal Peoples and oral and written expression (core)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area examines how Aboriginal Peoples' human rights and fundamental entitlement to self-determination have been denied since invasion, and the relationship between land rights and Aboriginal Communities' autonomy.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Key concepts of human rights, self-determination and autonomy

Human rights are classified into 3 categories:

  • civil and political rights – held by individuals
  • economic, social and cultural rights – held by individuals
  • collective human rights – held by whole communities and include the right to self-determination, the right to economic and social development, the right to communicate, and the right to a healthy environment and natural resources.

Human rights are about social justice, ensuring the fair and equitable distribution of and access to economic, political, social and cultural rights and opportunities.

Self-determination and autonomy involve allowing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to have a say in all matters that affect them and to have an ongoing choice about what is best for them individually and collectively.

Collective human rights are important for Indigenous Peoples worldwide because many Indigenous Peoples often have a collective worldview, whereby their identity and wellbeing are defined in relation to the whole group.

Denial of human rights

Historically, Indigenous Peoples worldwide have been subjected to human rights violations by colonising powers. In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples were and are impacted by the legacies of invasion, colonisation and the subsequent denial of human rights. These impacts include:

  • inability to make decisions individually and collectively
  • prohibiting the recognition, practice and maintenance of Languages and Cultures
  • intergenerational trauma, including trauma experienced by survivors of the Stolen Generations, their families and Communities
  • disadvantages concerning education, health, employment, economic independence and experiences with law and justice systems.

To address past injustices and ongoing impacts, many Aboriginal Community-controlled organisations, advisory groups and advocacy groups have emerged. These are addressed further in the Aboriginal enterprises and organisations focus area.

Individuals and Communities are reclaiming and revitalising Cultural Knowledges and Practices such as:

  • Language, song, dance and ceremony
  • land and waterway management Practices.

Lands and waterways, economic independence and self-determination

  • As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have had an intrinsic connection to lands and waterways since the beginning of the Dreaming.
  • Waterways may be described as Saltwater and Freshwater Country, but may include lakes, billabongs, estuaries, and surrounding vegetation and landforms.
  • The land and its waterways contain the necessary resources from which Aboriginal Peoples have always sustainably built economic systems, including trade within and outside the continent.
  • Colonisation and dispossession changed the way many Aboriginal Peoples accessed the land, its waterways and resources. This impacted individual and Community opportunities for economic independence and self-determination.

Land rights

Land rights encapsulates the evolving struggle of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Indigenous Peoples worldwide for the absolute legal and moral acknowledgement of prior ownership of their land. This struggle also encompasses all accompanying rights and obligations that flow from this, including economic independence and self-determination.

Native Title

  • ‘Native Title’ is the name given by the High Court to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander property rights recognised by the court in the Mabo judgement. See Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1.
  • The High Court’s Wik judgement (Wik Peoples v The State of Queensland; The Thayorre People v The State of Queensland [1996] HCA 40) decided an issue left unresolved by the Mabo judgement when it determined that native title could coexist with other rights on land held under a pastoral lease.
  • Increasingly, the definition is governed by the terms of the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), amended in 1998.
  • Native Title as recognised by Australian law does not cover the full scope of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ relationship to Country/Place under their laws and has been characterised as ‘recognition space’ between Customary law and Australian law.
  • ‘Native Title’ (capitalised) refers to the legislation, whereas ‘native title’ (lower case) refers to the concept.

  • advocacy
  • autonomy
  • Cultural expression(s)
  • freehold title
  • genocide
  • human rights
  • Indigenous Land Use Agreement (ILUA)
  • Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs)
  • land rights
  • Mabo
  • missions
  • Native Title/native title
  • reserves
  • self-determination
  • Stolen Generations
  • terra nullius
  • United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)

Suggested case studies

A case study on the activities of organisations, movements and individuals who have worked towards Aboriginal Peoples' autonomy and the broader Community response can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • Aboriginal Tent Embassy
  • 1967 Referendum.

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of issues that have arisen post-invasion and which impact Aboriginal Peoples' demands for self-determination.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for the development of numeracy skills that are relevant to this focus area. For example, analysing data related to population changes in Aboriginal Communities, using maps to record Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land usage and ownership, or exploring timelines that represent the chronology of events and their impacts.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy (core)

system.name: MS S4 Teaching advice for Aboriginal self-determination and autonomy (core)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

This focus area examines how Aboriginal Peoples' human rights and fundamental entitlement to self-determination have been denied since invasion, and the relationship between land rights and Aboriginal Communities' autonomy.

Aboriginal Community consultation should be undertaken to ensure that the examples selected are appropriate for the school and local Aboriginal Community context.

Key concepts of human rights, self-determination and autonomy

Human rights are classified into 3 categories:

  • civil and political rights – held by individuals
  • economic, social and cultural rights – held by individuals
  • collective human rights – held by whole communities and include the right to self-determination, the right to economic and social development, the right to communicate, and the right to a healthy environment and natural resources.

Human rights are about social justice, ensuring the fair and equitable distribution of and access to economic, political, social and cultural rights and opportunities.

Self-determination and autonomy involve allowing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to have a say in all matters that affect them and to have an ongoing choice about what is best for them individually and collectively.

Collective human rights are important for Indigenous Peoples worldwide because many Indigenous Peoples often have a collective worldview, whereby their identity and wellbeing are defined in relation to the whole group.

Denial of human rights

Historically, Indigenous Peoples worldwide have been subjected to human rights violations by colonising powers. In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples were and are impacted by the legacies of invasion, colonisation and the subsequent denial of human rights. These impacts include:

  • inability to make decisions individually and collectively
  • prohibiting the recognition, practice and maintenance of Languages and Cultures
  • intergenerational trauma, including trauma experienced by survivors of the Stolen Generations, their families and Communities
  • disadvantages concerning education, health, employment, economic independence and experiences with law and justice systems.

To address past injustices and ongoing impacts, many Aboriginal Community-controlled organisations, advisory groups and advocacy groups have emerged. These are addressed further in the Aboriginal enterprises and organisations focus area.

Individuals and Communities are reclaiming and revitalising Cultural Knowledges and Practices such as:

  • Language, song, dance and ceremony
  • land and waterway management Practices.

Lands and waterways, economic independence and self-determination

  • As the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world, Aboriginal Peoples have had an intrinsic connection to lands and waterways since the beginning of the Dreaming.
  • Waterways may be described as Saltwater and Freshwater Country, but may include lakes, billabongs, estuaries, and surrounding vegetation and landforms.
  • The land and its waterways contain the necessary resources from which Aboriginal Peoples have always sustainably built economic systems, including trade within and outside the continent.
  • Colonisation and dispossession changed the way many Aboriginal Peoples accessed the land, its waterways and resources. This impacted individual and Community opportunities for economic independence and self-determination.

Land rights

Land rights encapsulates the evolving struggle of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Indigenous Peoples worldwide for the absolute legal and moral acknowledgement of prior ownership of their land. This struggle also encompasses all accompanying rights and obligations that flow from this, including economic independence and self-determination.

Native Title

  • ‘Native Title’ is the name given by the High Court to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander property rights recognised by the court in the Mabo judgement. See Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1.
  • The High Court’s Wik judgement (Wik Peoples v The State of Queensland; The Thayorre People v The State of Queensland [1996] HCA 40) decided an issue left unresolved by the Mabo judgement when it determined that native title could coexist with other rights on land held under a pastoral lease.
  • Increasingly, the definition is governed by the terms of the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), amended in 1998.
  • Native Title as recognised by Australian law does not cover the full scope of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ relationship to Country/Place under their laws and has been characterised as ‘recognition space’ between Customary law and Australian law.
  • ‘Native Title’ (capitalised) refers to the legislation, whereas ‘native title’ (lower case) refers to the concept.

Key terms

  • advocacy
  • autonomy
  • Cultural expression(s)
  • freehold title
  • genocide
  • human rights
  • Indigenous Land Use Agreement (ILUA)
  • Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs)
  • land rights
  • Mabo
  • missions
  • Native Title/native title
  • reserves
  • self-determination
  • Stolen Generations
  • terra nullius
  • United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)

Suggested case studies

A case study on the activities of organisations, movements and individuals who have worked towards Aboriginal Peoples' autonomy and the broader Community response can be included in this focus area. Suggested case studies include:

  • Aboriginal Tent Embassy
  • 1967 Referendum.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Recognising the background knowledge, experiences and understanding that students with diverse lived experiences may bring to this focus area.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, including accessible resources and visual or digital aids to communicate and demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports and to use their home language or dialect when generating ideas and planning for tasks and activities.
  • Extending students by encouraging analysis of issues that have arisen post-invasion and which impact Aboriginal Peoples' demands for self-determination.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for the development of numeracy skills that are relevant to this focus area. For example, analysing data related to population changes in Aboriginal Communities, using maps to record Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land usage and ownership, or exploring timelines that represent the chronology of events and their impacts.
